quote: Soll eine Form $f$ $n^{ter}$ Ordnung als Summe von {+($n^{ten}$)+} Potenzen von Linearformen dargestellt werden, so fragt es sich, [-ob-] wie vieldeutig diese Darstellung ist.
english: If a form f of order n is to be represented as a sum of (n-th) powers of linear forms, the question arises how far from unique (how many-valued) this representation is.
topic: Hilbert rejects the view, said to be held in Berlin, that his invariant-theory work merely transfers Kronecker's ideas, and he then begins discussing how many ways a form of order n can be written as a sum of n-th powers of linear forms.

triage.modern_statement: Waring decomposition and identifiability of forms. Take a form f of degree n in several variables over C. Write it as a sum of n-th powers of linear forms, f = L_1^n + ... + L_r^n. How many such decompositions exist? In particular, for a general form with the minimal (generic) number of summands r, is the decomposition unique up to reordering and scaling of the summands? Today this property is called 'identifiability', and the number of decompositions is the 'Waring decomposition count'. The note itself only asks the question and does not say which number of variables or degree Hilbert meant.
triage.answered_by: Partial classical answers came first. Sylvester (1851) treated binary forms and, with his Pentahedral Theorem, quaternary cubics as unique sums of 5 cubes. Ternary quintics, uniquely sums of 7 fifth powers, were done by Hilbert himself (1888), Palatini (1903) and Richmond (1904), with a modern treatment by Massarenti–Mella (2013). The general case was finished by F. Galuppi and M. Mella, 'Identifiability of homogeneous polynomials and Cremona transformations' (arXiv:1606.06895, 2016; J. reine angew. Math.). They found every degree and number of variables for which a general form has a unique Waring decomposition.

evidence.claim: Survey (Arnold Math. J.): in modern terms, the cases where the general form of a given degree has a unique decomposition up to permutation are called identifiable. The known cases are the quaternary cubics (Sylvester's Pentahedral Theorem) and the ternary quintics (Hilbert 1888b, Palatini 1903, Richmond 1904, Massarenti–Mella 2013). Galuppi and Mella proved these are the only possible identifiable cases.

Galuppi–Mella say they 'conclude a work started more than a century ago' by describing all degrees d and numbers of variables n+1 for which a general polynomial is identifiable, i.e. has a unique additive decomposition into powers of linear forms.
Identifiability (uniqueness) of Waring decompositions of symmetric tensors is still studied with Hilbert-function methods, including cases where Kruskal's criterion does not apply.

triage.why: The note asks how far from unique the representation of a degree-n form as a sum of n-th powers of linear forms is. That is exactly the uniqueness ('identifiability') question for Waring decompositions, and Hilbert himself published the ternary-quintic case in 1888. For general forms the question was fully answered by Galuppi–Mella (2016/2017). It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Work continues on non-general forms, specific ranks, effective identifiability criteria and tensor applications. Confidence is medium, not high, because the note is short and does not fix the number of variables or the number of summands, so tying it to exactly this line of work is an interpretation.
